lesson.title: Pricing Effects in Sales and Cost Forecasts
lesson.summary: Sales and costs are driven by both quantities and prices, so a good forecast models each separately and shows how rising or falling prices move revenue, costs and margins. This matters because inflation or deflation can raise or shrink profits even when the business sells exactly the same number of units.

sections.heading: Start with sales = price × quantity
sections.body_markdown:
Think of a pizza shop. Revenue rises if it sells more pizzas, if it charges more per pizza, or both. A forecaster therefore builds sales from two pieces: **volume** (units sold) and **price** (average selling price per unit).

**Nominal** figures are measured in the money of the day and include price changes. **Real** figures strip price changes out and show only the change in quantity. A forecast of sales in currency is a nominal forecast, so it must carry a view on prices as well as units.

Price assumptions should reflect the industry and the product. A general inflation figure is only a starting point, because different products and inputs have different price trends.

sections.heading: Combining volume growth and price growth
sections.body_markdown:
If volume grows at rate $g_v$ and price grows at rate $g_p$, sales grow by the two growth factors multiplied together:

$$1+g_{sales}=(1+g_v)(1+g_p)$$

So 4% volume growth and 3% price growth give $1.04\times1.03-1=7.12\%$ nominal growth, not 7%. The extra 0.12% is the price rise applied to the extra units. Going the other way, real (volume) growth is nominal growth deflated by the price change: $(1+g_{nominal})/(1+g_p)-1$.

**Deflation** means prices fall, so $g_p$ is negative. Technology products are a classic case. Unit sales must then grow faster than prices fall for revenue to rise at all. Company sales can also be built as industry sales × market share, with the industry figure itself built from volume and price.

sections.heading: Costs: not everything inflates the same way or at the same time
sections.body_markdown:
Costs react to price changes in different ways.

- **Variable costs** (materials, direct labor) move with volume and also with the prices of those inputs. Forecast them as units × input price per unit, not just as a fixed percentage of sales.
- **Fixed costs** (rent, managers' salaries) do not move with volume, but they can still rise with inflation, for example when a lease is renewed or salaries are reviewed. Forecast them from their own dollar history and contract terms.

Two questions decide what happens to profit. First, how fast does each cost rise compared with selling prices? Second, can the company pass cost increases on to customers? A firm with strong **pricing power** can raise prices as costs rise and keep margins steady. A firm with weak pricing power sees margins squeezed. Contracts, hedges and delays between a cost change and a price change all shift timing.

Use price series that match the company's own inputs and products, such as commodity, wage or producer prices. A headline consumer index covers a different basket and may be distorted by volatile food and energy items.

sections.heading: Reading the reported numbers and testing the forecast
sections.body_markdown:
Accounting choices affect how price changes show up in reported results. When purchase costs rise, FIFO inventory costing sends the older, cheaper costs to cost of goods sold. This gives a higher reported gross profit and a higher inventory balance than LIFO. When purchase costs fall, the effect reverses. The company is no different economically, so be careful when comparing companies that use different methods.

Because price paths are uncertain, build the forecast with inflation as an explicit input and run scenarios: normal, high-inflation and deflation cases. A change in one assumption then ripples through revenue, costs and margin, and shows how sensitive profit is to price assumptions.

worked_example.problem: A company sold 500,000 units at $20 each last year, so revenue was $10,000,000. The analyst expects volume to grow 4% a year and the average selling price to grow 3% a year, both compounded annually. Forecast revenue two years from now.
steps: Combine the two growth factors for one year: $1.04\times1.03=1.0712$, so nominal revenue grows 7.12% a year.
Check: year-1 revenue is $520,000 \text{ units}\times\$20.60=\$10,712,000$, which equals $10,000,000\times1.0712$.
BA II Plus: press 2nd CLR TVM to clear. Then 10000000 +/- PV; 2 N; 7.12 I/Y; 0 PMT; CPT FV.
The calculator shows about 11,474,694.4 (ignore the sign).

formulas.name: Nominal sales growth from volume and price
formulas.where: g_sales = nominal sales growth rate; g_v = growth rate of unit volume; g_p = growth rate of average price (negative under deflation).

formulas.name: Real (volume) growth from nominal growth
formulas.where: g_real = growth after removing price changes; g_nominal = growth in sales in current currency; g_p = price change over the same period.

formulas.name: Price or cost path with constant inflation
formulas.where: P_t = price or unit cost after t periods; P_0 = current price or cost; g_p = per-period price change (negative for deflation); t = number of periods.

exam_traps: Adding volume growth and price growth instead of multiplying the factors; this understates nominal growth.
Applying one economy-wide inflation rate to every revenue and cost line, ignoring that each product and input has its own price trend.
Assuming selling prices and input costs always move together; whether they do depends on pricing power, contracts and timing.
Forecasting fixed costs as a percentage of sales when they follow contracts and their own dollar history.
Mixing real and nominal figures, for example comparing nominal sales growth to unit growth and calling the gap 'efficiency'.

mcqs.stem: An analyst wants to forecast nominal sales for a company in an industry where prices are expected to change. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Forecast units only, since price changes affect costs rather than revenue
options.explanation: Wrong: price changes affect revenue directly because sales equal price times quantity. Ignoring them leaves out half the driver.

options.text: Apply the economy-wide inflation rate to every revenue and cost line
options.explanation: Wrong: this ignores that products and inputs have their own price trends, so one rate misstates both revenue and costs.

options.text: Forecast volume and price separately, then combine them into nominal sales
options.explanation: Correct: sales are price times quantity, so each driver gets its own assumption and the two are combined.

mcqs.stem: Industry sales are $800 million today. Over the next three years, unit volume is expected to grow 2% a year and average selling prices 5% a year, each compounded annually. Using the combined annual growth rate, what are industry sales at the end of year 3? Round to two decimals, in $ millions.

options.explanation: Mistake: adding 2% and 5% to get 7% growth, which drops the interaction term. The combined rate is 1.02 × 1.05 − 1 = 7.1%.
Correct: combined growth is 1.02 × 1.05 − 1 = 7.1%, and 800 × 1.071^3 ≈ 982.78.
Mistake: compounding volume growth only (800 × 1.02^3) and ignoring the price increase.

mcqs.stem: A company's input costs are expected to rise faster than the prices it can charge customers because competition limits its pricing power. All else equal, how should the analyst forecast its gross margin?

options.text: Lower, because cost of goods sold grows faster than the prices it can charge
options.explanation: Correct: when costs rise faster than prices and cannot be passed on, gross profit per unit shrinks and the margin narrows.

options.text: Unchanged, because cost of goods sold is always a fixed share of sales
options.explanation: Mistake: holding the historical cost percentage fixed assumes full pass-through, which this company lacks.

options.text: Higher, because inflation raises nominal sales and so profit
options.explanation: Mistake: nominal sales rise only as fast as the company's own prices. Costs here rise faster, so the margin does not widen.

mcqs.stem: A company's nominal sales are forecast to grow 9.18% next year. Over the same year its average selling prices are expected to rise 6.00%. What real (volume) growth is implied? Round to two decimals in percent.

options.explanation: Mistake: subtracting 6.00% from 9.18%. Growth rates are factors, so the price change must be divided out, not subtracted.
Mistake: multiplying by the price factor (1.0918 × 1.06 − 1) instead of dividing by it.
Correct: 1.0918 / 1.06 − 1 = 3.00%, which is the volume growth after removing the price rise.

mcqs.stem: A segment sells products whose average prices fall steadily every year because of technological progress. For its nominal sales to rise, which condition is needed?

options.text: Sales must fall, because falling prices always outweigh changes in units sold
options.explanation: Mistake: this treats deflation as a guaranteed revenue decline. Revenue also depends on volume.

options.text: Unit volume must grow faster than the rate at which prices fall
options.explanation: Correct: nominal growth is (1 + volume growth)(1 + price change) − 1, so it is positive only if volume growth exceeds the price decline.

options.text: Sales will rise whenever unit volume rises, because price declines only affect costs
options.explanation: Mistake: price declines hit revenue directly. Units rising by less than prices fall still reduces sales.

mcqs.stem: A product sells for $500 today. Because of technology improvement, its average price is expected to fall 8% per year, compounded annually. What is the expected price at the end of year 3? Round to two decimals.

options.explanation: Correct: each year the price is multiplied by 0.92, so 500 × 0.92^3 ≈ 389.34.
Mistake: applying a simple 24% decline (3 × 8%) to the starting price instead of compounding on the falling price.
Mistake: dividing by 1.08^3, as if discounting, instead of multiplying by 0.92 each year.

mcqs.stem: An analyst is choosing inflation assumptions for a manufacturer's cost lines (metals, factory wages) and its product prices. Which approach is most defensible?

options.text: Use price series matching the company's own inputs and products, such as commodity, wage or producer prices
options.explanation: Correct: costs and prices follow the specific baskets the company buys and sells, so matching series give better forecasts than a general index.

options.text: Use headline consumer price inflation for every line because it covers the widest basket of goods
options.explanation: Mistake: the consumer basket differs from the company's inputs and products, and headline figures include volatile food and energy items.

options.text: Set input-cost inflation to zero in any year when the company's selling prices are rising
options.explanation: Mistake: rising selling prices do not mean input costs are flat. Costs and prices follow separate drivers and timing.

mcqs.stem: A manufacturer's key input costs $12.00 per unit today. The analyst expects the price of that input to rise 5% a year, compounded annually. What is the expected input cost per unit at the end of year 4? Round to two decimals.

options.explanation: Mistake: applying simple growth of 4 × 5% = 20% to $12.00 instead of compounding each year.
Mistake: compounding for only 3 periods (12 × 1.05^3) instead of 4.

flashcards.front: How do you build nominal sales from price and volume when both change?
flashcards.back: Multiply the growth factors: 1 + g_sales = (1 + g_volume)(1 + g_price). Do not just add the rates.

flashcards.front: How do you find real (volume) growth from nominal sales growth and a price change?
flashcards.back: Divide out the price factor: (1 + nominal growth) / (1 + price change) − 1.

flashcards.front: Why is pricing power central to forecasting margins when input costs rise?
flashcards.back: A firm that can pass cost increases on to customers keeps its margin. A firm that cannot sees costs outrun prices and its margin narrows.

flashcards.front: When purchase costs are rising, how does FIFO compare with LIFO on reported gross profit and inventory?
flashcards.back: FIFO sends older, cheaper costs to cost of goods sold, so it reports higher gross profit and higher ending inventory. The effects reverse when costs fall.
